title: ser and estar
summary: Catalan has two verbs for “to be”: which one to use when.
explanation:
English has one verb to be; Catalan splits it into two: ser and estar.

ser says what a person or thing is: name, origin, profession, character, material, price, time — and also where something is located:

  • Jo soc de Londres. — I’m from London.
  • El bany és al fons. — The bathroom is at the end (of the corridor).

estar describes a state (physical or emotional) and staying somewhere for a period of time:

  • Estic cansat. — I’m tired.
  • Aquest mes estem a Girona. — This month we’re (staying) in Girona.

Careful if you have learned some Spanish: unlike Spanish, Catalan normally uses ser for the location of things: On és l’estació? — Where is the station? Here estar means “to stay, to spend some time”: Hi estarem dues setmanes. — We’ll stay there for two weeks.

Two more differences from English: Catalan doesn’t express it as a subject (És car. — It’s expensive), and clock time is plural: Són les tres. — It’s three o’clock (but És la una — It’s one o’clock).

Forms:

  • ser: soc, ets, és, som, sou, són
  • estar: estic, estàs, està, estem, esteu, estan

Since the 2016 spelling reform the first person is written without an accent — soc; the form sóc still appears in older texts and dictionaries. The accent on és and són remains (unit 53).

examples.en: How are you? — Very well, thanks.

examples.ca: El mercat és a la plaça.
examples.en: The market is in the square.

title: Present tense of regular verbs
summary: Three conjugations — -ar, -er/-re, -ir — and two patterns for -ir verbs.
explanation:
Catalan verbs fall into three conjugations according to the ending of the infinitive. Where English adds an ending only in the third person (I speak, she speaks), Catalan has a different ending for every person — which is why the subject pronoun is usually left out: parlo on its own means “I speak”.

1. -ar (parlar — to speak): parlo, parles, parla, parlem, parleu, parlen

2. -er / -re (perdre — to lose): perdo, perds, perd, perdem, perdeu, perden

3. -ir has two patterns:

  • pure (like dormir — to sleep): dormo, dorms, dorm, dormim, dormiu, dormen
  • with the insert -eix- (like servir — to serve): serveixo, serveixes, serveix, servim, serviu, serveixen

Most -ir verbs follow the -eix- pattern: llegir → llegeixo, decidir → decideixo, afegir → afegeixo. Only a small group are “pure”: dormir, sentir, obrir, omplir, fugir, collir, sortir, tossir.

Note: the 1st person singular ends in -o (parlo), while the 3rd person singular is the shortest form, with no personal ending (parla, perd, dorm).

One present form covers all the English presents: parlo = I speak, I’m speaking, I do speak. And there is no “do” in questions or negatives: Parles anglès? — Do you speak English?

examples.en: I read the newspaper every morning.

title: hi ha: “there is” and “there are”
summary: Saying that something exists — and how hi ha differs from ser.
explanation:
hi ha is the Catalan for there is and there are. Unlike English, it never changes for number — the same form for singular and plural:

  • Hi ha un llibre damunt la taula. — There’s a book on the table.
  • Hi ha molts llibres a casa. — There are a lot of books at home.

Don’t make it agree with a plural noun: hi han is heard in casual speech, but it is not standard.

The negative is no hi ha; a question simply uses rising intonation, with no word-order change as in is there…?:

  • No hi ha llet. — There’s no milk.
  • Hi ha una farmàcia a prop? — Is there a pharmacy nearby?

Other tenses: hi havia (there was / there were — a description), hi va haver (there was — something happened), hi haurà (there will be), hi ha hagut (there has been / there have been).

hi ha or ser? The contrast is the same as English there is versus is: hi ha says that something exists (usually with an indefinite article or no article), while ser says where a particular, known thing is:

  • Hi ha un gat al jardí. — There’s a cat in the garden.
  • El gat és al jardí. — The cat is in the garden.

Note also that gent (people) is singular in Catalan: Hi ha molta gent. — There are a lot of people.

examples.ca: Hi ha molta gent a la plaça.
examples.en: There are a lot of people in the square.

examples.ca: Hi havia neu a la muntanya.
examples.en: There was snow in the mountains.

title: The definite article: el, la, els, les
summary: Four words for “the”, l’ before a vowel, and contractions with prepositions.
explanation:
English has one definite article, the; Catalan has four, because the article agrees with the noun in gender and number. As in English, it shows that the thing is known from the context.

  • masculine: el llibre → els llibres
  • feminine: la casa → les cases

Before a vowel or h in the singular, el and la become l’: l’home, l’escola, l’hotel, l’amiga.

Exception: there is no apostrophe before feminine words beginning with an unstressed i- or u- (also hi-, hu-): la Irene, la universitat, la història.

The article combines with the prepositions a, de, per:

  • a + el = al; a + els = als
  • de + el = del; de + els = dels
  • per + el = pel; per + els = pels

la, les and l’ never contract: a la casa, de les noies, a l’escola.

Catalan also uses the article where English doesn’t: for things in general (M’agrada la música. — I like music) and, in everyday Central Catalan, before people’s first names: en Joan, la Maria, l’Anna.

examples.en: The book belongs to the school.

examples.ca: La Maria i en Joan són germans.
examples.en: Maria and Joan are brother and sister.

title: The indefinite article: un, una, uns, unes
summary: When to use un/una — and when Catalan has no article where English says “a”.
explanation:
The indefinite article introduces something that hasn’t been mentioned yet, like English a/an. It agrees with the noun:

  • masculine: un gos → uns gossos
  • feminine: una casa → unes cases

The plurals uns / unes mean “some”, “a few”: unes amigues — some (female) friends. There is no a/an switch: un home, una amiga.

No article is used:

  • before a profession after ser — the classic slip for English speakers: Soc professor. — I’m a teacher (but with an adjective the article returns: És un metge molt bo. — He’s a very good doctor);
  • before uncountable substances, where English often says some: Vull aigua. — I want some water;
  • after a negative, cap (“no, not any”) is often used: No tinc cap germà. — I don’t have any brothers.

examples.ca: Tinc un gos i una gata.
examples.en: I have a dog and a (female) cat.

examples.ca: Hi ha unes cadires al jardí.
examples.en: There are some chairs in the garden.

exercises.instruction: Fill in un, una, uns, unes — or a dash if no article is needed.

title: Noun gender
summary: How to tell masculine from feminine — and what to do about the exceptions.
explanation:
English nouns have no grammatical gender — a table is just “it”. In Catalan every noun, even an object or an idea, is masculine or feminine, and that decides the form of the article and the adjective. The best habit is to learn every noun together with its article. As a rule:

  • nouns in -a are feminine: la casa, la taula, la poma;
  • nouns in a consonant or in -e, -o are masculine: el carrer, el cotxe, el metro;
  • nouns in -ció, -sió, -tat, -esa, and abstract nouns in -or made from adjectives, are feminine: l’estació, la televisió, la ciutat, la bellesa, la foscor (darkness). Note that l’ hides the gender: l’estació is feminine.

Male/female pairs are usually formed by adding -a: noi → noia, gat → gata, professor → professora. Sometimes, as in English, the word is different: home → dona (man, woman), pare → mare (father, mother), rei → reina (king, queen).

Learn the exceptions — masculine nouns in -a: el dia, el mapa, el problema, el tema, el sistema, el programa; and a few feminine nouns in -o that are shortened words: la foto, la moto, la ràdio.

Nouns in -ista are the same for both genders; only the article tells you who is meant: el dentista / la dentista.

exercises.instruction: Fill in el or la (or l’ before a vowel).

title: Plural of nouns
summary: How to form the plural, and the spelling changes that come with it.
explanation:
As in English, the general rule is to add -s: llibre → llibres, carrer → carrers. What is new for English speakers is the spelling changes.

Words in -a take -es instead, and may change their spelling to keep the same sound:

  • casa → cases
  • g → gu: amiga → amigues
  • c → qu: època → èpoques
  • ç → c: plaça → places
  • j → g: pluja → pluges

Many words ending in a stressed vowel add -ns: mà → mans, pa → pans, veí → veïns.

Masculine words in -s, -ç, -x, -ix, -tx add -os (compare English box → boxes): gas → gasos, braç → braços, peix → peixos. Some of them also double the s: gos → gossos, nas → nassos.

examples.en: I’m buying two loaves of bread.

title: Adjectives: gender, number and position
summary: Adjectives agree with the noun and usually come after it.
explanation:
In English an adjective never changes and comes before the noun: a new car, new cars. In Catalan it agrees with the noun in gender and number and usually comes after it:

  • un cotxe nou — a new car (masc.)
  • una casa nova — a new house (fem.)
  • uns cotxes nous, unes cases noves — new cars, new houses

Many adjectives form the feminine with -a: petit → petita, bo → bona, car → cara. Others are the same for both genders: gran, fàcil, difícil, feliç, intel·ligent.

A few adjectives change their meaning slightly when placed before the noun: un gran home (a great man) versus un home gran (an old man).

Two traps: adjectives of nationality have no capital letter (uns amics catalans — some Catalan friends), and simpàtic is a false friend — it means “nice, friendly”, not “sympathetic”.

exercises.instruction: Make the adjective agree with the noun.

title: Possessives: el meu, la meva…
summary: Possessives are used with the article and agree with the thing owned.
explanation:
English says my book; Catalan says, literally, “the my book”: the possessive almost always comes with the article:

  • my: el meu / la meva / els meus / les meves
  • your (tu): el teu / la teva / els teus / les teves
  • his, her, its: el seu / la seva / els seus / les seves
  • our: el nostre / la nostra / els nostres / les nostres
  • your (vosaltres): el vostre / la vostra / els vostres / les vostres
  • their: el seu / la seva / els seus / les seves

The form agrees with the thing owned, not with the owner. English his/her tells you about the owner; Catalan el seu / la seva doesn’t: la seva germana can be his, her or their sister (or your sister, if you address someone as vostè). In the same way, la meva germana (my sister) is feminine even when a man is speaking.

After ser the article is usually dropped, which gives the equivalent of English mine, yours, ours: Aquest llibre és meu. — This book is mine. Likewise: un amic meu — a friend of mine.

examples.ca: El meu pare treballa a Lleida.
La seva filla té cinc anys.
examples.en: Their daughter is five (or: his / her daughter).

title: Demonstratives: aquest and aquell
summary: “This” and “that”, plus the neuter forms això and allò.
explanation:
Like English this and that, Catalan distinguishes near and far — but the words agree with the noun in gender and number:

  • aquest / aquesta / aquests / aquestes — this, these (near me);
  • aquell / aquella / aquells / aquelles — that, those (further away).

When the thing isn’t named — you don’t know what it is, or you mean a situation or an idea — Catalan uses the neuter forms això (this) and allò (that). English uses this/that for both cases, so this distinction has to be learned:

  • Què és això? — What’s this?
  • Allò no m’agrada. — I don’t like that.

aquell also points back in time, like English those days: en aquella època — at that time.

Balearic and parts of Valencian have a three-way system, aquest — aqueix — aquell, but standard Catalan in Catalonia uses two.

title: Question words
summary: què, qui, quin, on, quan, com, quant, per què.
explanation:
The main question words:

  • què — what: Què fas? — What are you doing?
  • qui — who: Qui és? — Who is it?
  • quin / quina / quins / quines — which, what + noun (agrees with the noun): Quina hora és? — What time is it?
  • on — where: On vas? — Where are you going?
  • quan — when: Quan arribes? — When do you arrive?
  • com — how: Com estàs? — How are you?
  • quant / quanta / quants / quantes — how much, how many: Quants anys tens? — How old are you? (literally “how many years do you have?”)
  • per què — why (the answer “because” is perquè, one word): Per què no vens? — Perquè treballo. — Why aren’t you coming? — Because I’m working.

Three traps for English speakers:

  • No “do”: a question uses the same verb form as a statement, and the subject often follows the verb: On viu la Marta? — Where does Marta live?
  • What + noun is quin, not què: Quin llibre llegeixes? — What book are you reading?
  • A preposition can’t be left at the end of the question; it goes before the question word: D’on ets? — Where are you from? Amb qui parles? — Who are you talking to?

examples.ca: Com et dius? — Em dic Laura.
examples.en: What’s your name? — My name’s Laura.
How many brothers and sisters do you have?

title: Negation: no, mai, res, ningú, cap
summary: In Catalan a double negative is correct — and usually required.
explanation:
no goes straight before the verb, with no helper like English don’t: No parlo alemany. — I don’t speak German.

The negative words mai (never), res (nothing), ningú (nobody), cap (no, not any), gens (not at all) are used together with no. In standard English a double negative is wrong (I didn’t see nobody); in Catalan it is the norm:

  • No hi ha ningú. — There’s nobody here.
  • No menjo mai carn. — I never eat meat.
  • No tinc cap problema. — I don’t have any problems.

So where English says not … anybody, anything, any, Catalan says no … ningú, res, cap.

If the negative word comes before the verb, no becomes optional: Ningú (no) ho sap. — Nobody knows. Both versions are correct; the one with no is more traditional.

The word pas adds emphasis, mostly in writing and in some regions: No ho sé pas. — I really don’t know.

examples.ca: No hi ha cap taula lliure.
examples.en: There isn’t a single free table.

exercises.instruction: Make the sentence negative.

title: estar + gerund: what’s happening right now
summary: How to form the progressive, and why Catalan uses it less than English.
explanation:
To stress that an action is in progress at this very moment, Catalan uses estar + gerundi, the equivalent of English be + -ing:

  • Estic parlant amb la meva mare. — I’m talking to my mother (right now).

The gerund is formed like this:

  • -ar → -ant: parlar → parlant
  • -er/-re → -ent: perdre → perdent
  • -ir → -int: dormir → dormint

A few gerunds are irregular: fer → fent, dir → dient, veure → veient, escriure → escrivint, viure → vivint, beure → bevent.

Careful: Catalan uses this form much less than English uses -ing. The simple present often does the job: Què fas? — What are you doing? For habits and ongoing situations the simple present is the norm: Treballo en una oficina — I work in an office (not estic treballant). And it is never used for future plans, as English is: I’m seeing Joan tomorrow — Demà veig en Joan.

examples.en: What are you doing? — I’m reading.

title: vaig menjar or vaig a menjar?
summary: The everyday past tense built with anar — and why the preposition a changes everything.
explanation:
The most common past tense in Catalan is formed with anar (to go) + infinitive. This is the passat perifràstic:

  • vaig menjar — I ate
  • vas menjar, va menjar, vam menjar, vau menjar, van menjar

The singular forms look like the present of anar, but the plural is special: vam, vau (the present is anem, aneu).

This is the biggest trap for English speakers: vaig menjar looks like “I’m going to eat”, but it means the opposite — I ate. Although anar means “to go”, the meaning here is purely past: Ahir vam anar al cinema. — Yesterday we went to the cinema.

Add the preposition a, though, and anar is a verb of motion and intention again — “to go (and) do something”:

  • Vaig a menjar. — I’m going to eat (I’m off to eat).
  • Vaig menjar. — I ate.

For a plain future with no idea of going anywhere, careful Catalan prefers the future tense (Menjaré a les dues. — I’m going to eat at two).

There is also a literary simple past (perfet simple): menjà, parlà. It is hardly ever heard in speech — today it lives mainly in literature and in the Balearic Islands.

examples.ca: Què vas fer el cap de setmana?
examples.en: What did you do at the weekend?
